author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Diagnose geometry that vanishes near widescreen edges
summary: Use an edge-panning route to distinguish widescreen culling from clipping, renderer loss, and ordinary draw distance; compare unpatched 4:3, serial-matched 16:9, and fixed-camera scenes before keeping a patch.
heroAlt: Official PCSX2 widescreen game capture with world geometry extending toward both screen edges

blocks.text: Track an object through the original 4:3 boundary

Widescreen can reveal world space the game never expected to display. An object that disappears exactly where the old 4:3 edge would have been is likely culled by game logic, while geometry sliced by the current viewport can indicate clipping or projection. Choose a stationary landmark near the side of the camera and pan slowly until it exits and re-enters. Record the title's serial, patch identity, aspect setting, and renderer before comparing.
Do not hide edge loss with zoom or overscan. Cropping the viewport conceals evidence and removes valid image content without correcting culling.

A landmark that crosses the former 4:3 edge under 16:9.

blocks.text: Separate game culling from renderer clipping

items: 1. Cold-boot unpatched 4:3 and record the landmark moving from center to outside the visible frame.
2. Enable the verified widescreen patch and repeat the same camera speed and position.
3. Mark the exact horizontal point where the object vanishes and whether its shadow, particle, or reflection disappears with it.
4. Keep the patch active but compare the supported hardware APIs at native resolution.
5. If both APIs lose the object at the old boundary, treat game culling as the leading cause rather than GPU performance.
6. Disable the patch while retaining 16:9 stretch briefly to distinguish projection changes from simple viewport distortion.
7. Play the fixed-camera scene and inspect actors or props newly exposed at the sides.
8. Keep the patch only if normal play does not reveal disruptive culling or scripted staging.

blocks.text: Games often avoid drawing objects outside their expected camera frustum. A widescreen patch may widen projection without expanding every culling rule. Renderer clipping tends to follow the active viewport or API, while game-side culling commonly follows an invisible original boundary across renderers.
A usable wide profile must retain world continuity during motion.

items: Landmarks remain present until they naturally leave the 16:9 frame.
Shadows and reflections do not detach before their source object.
Both left and right pans behave consistently.
Fixed-camera scenes do not expose missing actors or unfinished staging.
The serial-matched patch survives a cold boot without extra zoom.

blocks.text: Evidence that the wide mode is incomplete

items: Objects vanish at the former 4:3 boundary on every renderer: document patch culling limits.
Only one API clips triangles at the current edge: isolate a renderer issue.
Zoom conceals the defect but removes subtitles: restore uncropped output.
A patch for another revision behaves unpredictably: remove it before further testing.

blocks.text: Disable the widescreen patch, select 4:3, reset zoom and overscan, then cold-boot the edge route. Remove any user patch that does not match the executable CRC and verify the same landmark under the clean profile.
Draw distance is not always culling
Objects that disappear by camera distance rather than screen position may follow level-of-detail or draw-distance rules. Repeat the pan from two distances before classifying the boundary.
